elements.id-string-106: Using error mining tools, we release a new corrected versionof the treebank, which leads to improved downstream task performance.We show that corrections made to a small size treebank of ahighly variable language favorably impacts the performance of NLP models trained on it.We augment the treebank by adding NER annotations and offensive language detection, expanding its applicability in various NLP tasks.We homogenize tokenization across the dataset, analyze theimpact of proper tokenization on UD tasks and NER and conduct arealistic evaluation on predicted tokenization, includingNER evaluation.

elements.id-string-110: The Arabic language exhibits diglossia, where Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) is employed in formal contexts, while dialectal forms are used informally \cite{habash10intro}.
elements.id-string-111: Dialectal forms, which display significant variability across regions and predominantly exist in spoken form, lack standardized spelling when written.
elements.id-string-112: Many Arabic speakers employ the Latin script for transcribing their dialects online, using digits and symbols for phonemes not easily mapped to Latin letters \cite{seddah-etal-2020-building}.
elements.id-string-113: This written form, known as Arabizi and its North African variant, NArabizi, often showcases code-switching with French and Amazigh \cite{amazouz2017addressing}.
elements.id-string-114: Textual resources for Arabizi primarily consist of noisy, user-generated content \cite{foster-2010-cba,seddah-etal-2012-french,eisenstein2013bad}, complicating the creation of supervised models or collection of extensive pre-training datasets.
elements.id-string-115: The original NArabizi treebank  \cite{seddah-etal-2020-building}, contains about 1500 sentences.
elements.id-string-116: The sentences are randomly sampled from the romanized Algerian dialectal Arabic corpus of \citet{cotterell2014algerian} and from a small corpus of lyrics from Algerian dialectal Arabic songs popular among the younger generation.
elements.id-string-117: This treebank is manually annotated with morpho-syntactic information (parts-of-speech and morphological features), together with glosses and code-switching labels at the word level, as well as sentence-level translations to French.

elements.id-string-153: \paragraph{Error Mining} We use the UD  validator Vr2.11 \footnote{\url{https://github.com/UniversalDependencies/tools/releases/tag/r2.11}}, a tool designed to assess the annotation of treebanks in UD and ensure compliance with the UD specifications.
elements.id-string-154: The validator is specifically employed to detect common errors, such as invalid dependency relations, incorrect part-of-speech tags, and inconsistent usage of features like tense and aspect.
elements.id-string-155: By leveraging the UD validator, we guarantee that our dataset is syntactically consistent and conforms to the standards established by the UD project.

elements.id-string-157: We also use Errator \cite{wisniewski2018errator}, a data mining tool, to pinpoint inconsistencies in our dataset.
elements.id-string-158: It implements the annotation principle presented by \citet{boyd2008detecting}, which suggests that if two identical word sequences have different annotations, one is likely erroneous.
elements.id-string-159: We remove the duplicated sentences when the text field is an exact match and fix duplicated sentence identification for different sentences.
elements.id-string-160: We also fixed some problems with the original text, such as Arabic characters encoding and sentence boundaries.
elements.id-string-161: \paragraph{Tokenization} We address tokenization concerns to uphold consistency in the NArabizi Treebank annotations.
elements.id-string-162: Furthermore, we introduce targeted adjustments to resolve issues related to segmenting specific word classes, including conjunctions, interjections (e.g., ``ya''), determiners, and prepositions, especially when adjacent to noun phrases.
elements.id-string-163: For example, we segment determiners at the initial vowel (``a'' or ``e''), as demonstrated in the examples ``e ssalam'' (``the peace'') and ``e dounoub'' (``the sins'').
elements.id-string-164: The lemma field for these terms is aligned with the French translation for the splitting (e.g., ``e ssalam'' $\Rightarrow$ ``la paix'' (``the peace'')).
elements.id-string-165: For prepositions, we perform splitting at the first letter followed by ``i'' when possible, as seen in ``brabi'' $\Rightarrow$ ``b rabi'' (``with my god'').
elements.id-string-166: We also establish rules for segmenting determiners and proper nouns.
elements.id-string-167: When possible, we separate prepositions at the initial letter and ``i'' and instituted guidelines for segmenting determiners and proper nouns.
elements.id-string-168: We implement these alterations for splitting using the Grew graph rewriting tool for NLP \cite{guillaume2021graph} to improve the consistency and quality of the treebank annotations.
elements.id-string-169: Additionally, we fix all the problems mentioned by \citet{touileb-barnes-2021-interplay} regarding the incoherence of the tokenization, wrong translations, and incoherent annotations.
elements.id-string-170: \paragraph{Translation} The translation quality is also enhanced; previously, translations were not consistently carried out by Algerian speakers, resulting in local expressions and phrases being frequently misinterpreted, either in a literal manner or, at times, entirely inaccurately.

elements.id-string-183: Our NER annotation guidelines are based on the revised tokenization of the NArabizi treebank, which ensures consistency between token-level annotations, an essential aspect of multi-task learning.
elements.id-string-184: We use the Inception tool \cite{klie2018inception} for our manual annotation by two native speakers, adhering to the IOB2 Scheme \cite{tjong-kim-sang-veenstra-1999-representing}.

elements.id-string-299: In this section, we investigate the tokenization influence on the enhanced NArabizi Treebank, with a particular emphasis on the homogenization of the tokenization \footnote{We follow the  terminology of UD where a tokenizer performs token segmentation (i.e. source tokens).} and its subsequent impact on our tasks.
elements.id-string-300: We also evaluate the models in a realistic scenario where gold tokenization is unavailable.
elements.id-string-301: We use the UDPipe tokenizer \cite{straka-etal-2016-udpipe} that employs a Gated Linear Units (GRUs) \cite{cho-etal-2014-learning} artificial neural network for the identification of token and sentence boundaries in plain text.
elements.id-string-302: It processes fixed-length segments of Unicode characters and assigns each character to one of three classes: token boundary follows, sentence boundary follows, or no boundary\draftremove{By leveraging GRUs and dropout for regularization, the tokenizer achieves efficient performance with reduced computational requirements}.
elements.id-string-303: The tokenizer is trained using the Adam stochastic optimization method, employing randomly shuffled input sentences to ensure effective tokenization across various NLP tasks.
elements.id-string-308: We conduct a 5-fold evaluation using the UDPipe tokenizer and assess its performance based on the token-level, multiword, and word-level scores.
elements.id-string-309: The results in Table \ref{tab:tokenization_eval} show high scores for the tokens and words F1 scores demonstrate the tokenizer's efficacy in handling various tokens and words, which shows that the tokenization for NArabizi is learnable.
elements.id-string-310: We also notice sub-optimal performance regarding multi-words, due to their random occurrence nature.\footnote{It is important to note that tokens refer to surface tokens (e.g., French ``au" counts as one token), while words represent syntactic words (``au" is split into two words, ``à" and ``le").}.

elements.id-string-320: \paragraph{Named Entity Recognition Evaluation on Non-Gold Tokenization}
elements.id-string-321: The conventional evaluation methodology for NER typically assigns entities to distinct token positions.
elements.id-string-322: Nevertheless, this method proves inadequate when the token count for evaluation differs from the number of gold tokens, which is almost always the case when processing user-generated content.
elements.id-string-323: As a result, we adopt the evaluation strategy devised by \citet{bareket-tsarfaty-2021-neural}, which associates entities with their forms instead of their indices.
elements.id-string-324: This approach yields F1 scores based on strict, exact matches of surface forms for entities, irrespective of the category distinctions, thereby offering a more accurate and reliable evaluation in scenarios with varying token counts.
elements.id-string-325: In other words, the gold and predicted NE spans must exhibit an exact match regarding their form, boundaries, and associated entity type.

elements.id-string-334: In this paper, we present a comprehensive study on the development and refinement of the NArabizi Treebank \cite{seddah-etal-2020-building} by improving its annotations, consistency, and tokenization, as well as providing new annotations for NER and offensive language.
elements.id-string-335: Our work contributes to the enhancement of the NArabizi Treebank, making it a valuable resource for research on low-resource languages and user-generated content with high variability.
elements.id-string-336: We explore the impact of tokenization on the refined NArabizi treebank, employing the UDPipe tokenizer for our evaluation.
elements.id-string-337: The results demonstrate the tokenizer's effectiveness in handling various tokens and multiword expressions.
elements.id-string-338: Our experiments show that training and testing on the NArabiziv2 improve the UD tasks performances.
elements.id-string-339: Furthermore, we show the impact of the tokenization for NER and UD tasks, and we report results using predicted tokenization for evaluation to estimate the models' performance on raw data.
elements.id-string-340: Future research could emphasize expanding the NArabizi Treebank \draftreplace{to encompass other linguistic phenomena}{towards other dialects} and examining the treebank's potential applications in various NLP tasks.
elements.id-string-341: Our dataset is made freely available as part of the new version of the Narabizi Treebank\footnote{\url{https://gitlab.inria.fr/ariabi/release-narabizi-treebank}}.
elements.id-string-342: The next release will additionally contain a set of other sentence translations  prepared by a Tunisian speaker.
elements.id-string-343: These translations will be interesting for cross-dialect studies, given that the Narabizi corpus is predominantly made of Algerian dialect.
